opus-5.5.text:
I think the two approaches attack the same bottleneck, the KV cache, from different directions.

MLA, the latent attention approach, keeps full global attention at every layer but compresses keys and values into a low-dimensional latent. You keep the expressiveness of dense attention, and every token can still see every other token in every layer, but the memory per token drops a lot. The cost is complexity. Decoding needs careful kernel engineering, the absorption tricks, and handling positional encoding in a decoupled way. Compute also still grows with context length, because you're still attending over everything. Memory gets cheaper, but the attention computation itself isn't free at very long contexts.

A hybrid design, mixing sliding-window layers with a smaller number of global attention layers, takes a more structural route. Most layers only look at a local window, so their KV cache is essentially constant no matter how long the context gets. Only the global layers pay the full long-context cost. That gives you very fast inference and a small memory footprint, and it's friendly to speculative decoding and high-throughput serving, which matters a lot when you care about agentic workloads with many long rollouts.

The worry with hybrid attention is always whether you lose long-range capability. What we found, and what I think many people underestimated, is that with the right ratio of local to global layers, plus some details like attention sinks or learnable biases so the local layers can "park" attention properly, long-context retrieval and reasoning hold up surprisingly well. The global layers carry the long-range information, and the local layers do most of the fine-grained work.

So my overall view is that it isn't about which one is strictly better. MLA is an elegant compression of full attention. Hybrid attention is a bet that most of the work doesn't need global attention at every layer. For the regime we care about, long context, fast decoding, and RL with very long trajectories, I think the hybrid approach gives a better efficiency–capability tradeoff. In the long run I wouldn't be surprised to see the ideas combined: compressed global layers together with cheap local layers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of them as two different answers to the same bottleneck, which is the KV cache. Once your context goes past a hundred thousand tokens, decoding stops being compute-bound and becomes memory-bandwidth-bound. Every token you generate has to read the entire cache, so whatever you do to shrink that cache translates almost directly into throughput.

MLA attacks it through compression. You project keys and values into a shared low-rank latent, cache only that latent, and reconstruct on the fly. The beauty is that every layer still sees the full context. You lose almost nothing in quality, and you get a cache that's maybe a tenth of the size of standard multi-head attention. The cost is that it's a fairly delicate design. The up-projection has to be absorbed into the query path to avoid recomputing, RoPE has to be split into a decoupled part because it doesn't commute with the compression, and all of that means your kernels are custom and your inference stack has to be built around it. It also doesn't change the asymptotics. The cache is smaller, but it still grows linearly with sequence length, and so does the attention compute at prefill.

The hybrid approach we took in MiMo is more structural. Most layers only attend to a sliding window of a few thousand tokens, and a minority of layers keep full global attention. For the local layers the cache is constant regardless of context length, so the cost of going from thirty-two thousand to a million tokens is almost entirely carried by the global layers. That's a different kind of win. You get real sublinear growth in memory and much cheaper prefill, and the layers themselves are standard, so existing attention kernels and paged caching work with very little modification.

The tradeoff is where information lives. With a hybrid, you are making a bet that most of what a token needs is local, and that the global layers are enough to carry long-range dependencies. In practice that bet mostly holds, but you have to be careful about the ratio, where you place the global layers, and how you train for it. If you pretrain mostly on short sequences and then bolt on long context, the global layers never really learn to do the retrieval job, and you see it on needle-in-a-haystack and on multi-document reasoning. We spent a lot of effort on the long-context phase of training precisely because of that. MLA doesn't have this failure mode, because nothing is being thrown away.

So my honest assessment is that MLA is the better choice when you want the model to behave exactly like a dense full-attention model and you're willing to own the inference stack. The hybrid is the better choice when the dominant workload is very long inputs, agentic loops, or large codebases, and you need the system to stay fast at the far end of the context window. And the two are not mutually exclusive. You can put MLA-style compression on the global layers of a hybrid and get both effects at once. I think that's actually where things are heading, because the real competition for the next generation isn't about attention quality on short benchmarks anymore. It's about who can serve a million tokens of context at a cost that makes agents economically viable.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: how much state you keep, and how much of that state you read for each new token. Those are related, but they create different inference bottlenecks.

I’d want to clarify what you mean by MA before attributing a specific design to it. But if the comparison is between compressing attention state and MiMo’s hybrid approach, the architectural tradeoff is fairly clear. Compression aims to make retained context cheaper. A hybrid of local and global attention instead limits access to the full context in some layers, while preserving broader access in others.

That can be attractive for long-context decoding, where repeatedly reading a large KV cache becomes expensive. The question is whether the global layers provide enough capacity for information to travel across distant parts of the sequence. Local coherence is one thing; reliably retrieving and combining scattered evidence is another.

So I wouldn’t judge either approach by its attention complexity alone. I’d compare time to first token, decoding latency, and memory use at the same context length, batch size, and quality target. Kernel efficiency and hardware utilization can change the outcome substantially. The better architecture is the one that delivers the latency savings while preserving the long-context behavior your application actually needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d first clarify what you mean by MA, because the architectural details matter. If you mean multi-head latent attention, the central tradeoff is between compressing the KV cache and reducing how much context each attention layer reads.

Latent attention preserves access to the full history while storing a compressed representation of keys and values. That can substantially reduce cache memory, but the speedup depends on how efficiently the inference kernels handle that representation. A smaller cache doesn’t automatically translate into proportionally lower latency.

A hybrid attention design mixes local and full attention. Local layers read a bounded window, which reduces memory traffic as the context grows, while full-attention layers provide access to distant tokens. The tradeoff is where and how often you provide that global access. Too little can make tasks requiring precise retrieval or connections across distant passages harder.

So I’d compare them under the same workload: time to first token, decoding latency, memory use at the target concurrency, and quality on tasks that actually require the long context. I wouldn’t declare a winner from cache size alone, and I’d want the specific MiMo configuration before making a stronger claim.
